text: Left alone, most systems either keep everything forever or get 'cleaned up' by an engineer without checking who still needs the data. Neither is a decision. Data retention is deciding, in advance, how long each category of data is kept.

Over-retention feels safe — 'we might need it someday' — but every extra year of customer data sitting around is another year of breach exposure. Under-retention is the opposite problem: deleting records before a legal or tax obligation expires. And a legal hold suspends the whole schedule the moment litigation is reasonably anticipated.

A usable retention schedule answers four questions, not one: what category of data this is, how long it's kept — stated as a real duration — what trigger event starts the clock, and what disposition action happens when the period ends: delete, anonymize, or archive.

The most common mistake is skipping the trigger event. 'Seven years' means nothing without a starting point. Seven years from when a record was created, versus seven years from when the customer relationship ended, produces very different deletion dates for someone who stayed ten years.
Next lesson: what happens when that clock runs out, or when someone asks you to delete their data early — data deletion and the right to erasure.
